newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Portugal to revolutionise ports.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Portugal to revolutionise ports.

text.p: Portugal is preparing to revolutionise its ports and hopes that the southern harbour of Sines will become "the Singapore of Europe", a major hub for long-distance container deliveries.

Under an ambitious proposal expected to receive cabinet approval by September, Portugal will convert its five main port authorities into public companies and open bidding for concessions for private contractors to operate the ports.

The biggest project will be the promotion of Sines, 200 km (125 miles) south of Lisbon, as the "Singapore of Europe", says Jose Manuel Consiglieri Pedroso, Deputy Minister for Planning and Public Works.

Benefiting from its location facing the Americas and Africa, a deep water terminal will be built at Sines capable of handling container deliveries of all kinds of produce. Presently Sines unloads coal and oil.
New road and rail links from Sines will ensure the efficient delivery of goods to Spain and the rest of Europe.

"We want to convert Sines into a major container port. Sines has an excellent location at the extreme western edge of Europe, and has a good climate and plenty of space for development," Consiglieri Pedroso told Reuters in an interview.

Portugal's Socialist government would launch a "road show" later this year to promote Sines to private investors around the world who could be interested in joining project financing to expand the port, he added.
FEARS SINES COULD TURN INTO A "WHITE ELEPHANT"

Antonio Mariano, president of the National Federation of Dockers' Unions, said he hoped Sines would be a success, but feared it might turn into a "white elephant" if shipowners continued to opt for northern European ports.
"Sines is far away from big cities and there are no guarantees that the big shipowners will dock there," he said.
The government plans to increase the depth and capacity of the waterway and container terminals at Lisbon and Setubal, and to lengthen the terminal at Aveiro.
"We want Lisbon and Setubal to be complementary, and to act as alternatives. If there were a problem at one port, the other could take over its activities," Consiglieri Pedroso said.
Setubal, 50 km (30 miles) south of Lisbon, is largely dedicated to unloading imported cars and parts for Portugal's car assembly industry, as well as exporting arms.
Road and rail links from all the ports will be improved to reduce congestion around the cities.
Portugal plans to invest nearly 100 billion escudos ($587 million) to modernise the infrastructure of its ports by the year 2000, Consiglieri Pedroso said.
The funds will include some 35 billion escudos from the state budget, 35 billion from self-financing and 30 billion from European Union (EU) structural funds, he added.
The investment will include up to 40 billion escudos for Sines, including 15 billion from state funds.
PORTS CONVERTED TO PUBLIC COMPANIES
According to the proposal, the main port authorities of Lisbon, Leixoes in the north, Aveiro in the centre, Setubal and Sines, will be converted into public companies.
"The creation of public companies will give more flexibility and autonomy to the ports," Consiglieri Pedroso said.

Mariano said he was unconvinced that the conversion of the ports into public companies would improve their efficiency and said that he feared it would encourage the hiring of casual labour, who lack adequate qualifications.
Portugal presently has around 750 dockers, all of whom are unionised, down from some 5,000 in 1989, according to union figures. Many were laid off because of the introduction of automation.

The secondary ports of Viana do Castelo and Figueira da Foz in the north and centre, and Portimao and Faro in the south will be reorganised with the creation of Port Institutes of the North, Centre and South, according to the proposal.

Consiglieri Pedroso said private contractors could begin operating port services in early 1998 after a public bidding process, but added that port infrastructure would not be privatised as no one would be interested in buying it.
"All operations by private contractors must be self-financing," he said.
So far only Sines was financing its own operations, he added. Lisbon and Leixoes ports are heavily indebted. ($ = 170.3 Portugese Escudos)
